about.title: Voltra — Electrical Panel Designer
about.subtitle: Design DIN rail electrical distribution boards and wiring schemes. Works offline, runs in your browser.

features.title: Features
items: Visual DIN rail panel editor with multi-rail layouts and configurable slot counts
Drag-and-drop palette of MCBs, RCDs, RCBOs, isolators, contactors, timers, SPDs, meters, sockets, lamps and more
Typed properties per device (rating, curve, sensitivity, poles, coil voltage, MID class, SPD type…)
Port-to-port wiring with a connection matrix and schematic view
Circuit tags, phase assignment (L1/L2/L3), labels, notes, and input cables
Undo / redo history (50 steps), snapshots, copy / paste, auto-numbering, auto-pack rails
Wiring schemes editor: switches, lamps, LEDs, sockets, transformers, motors, junctions with rotation
20+ electrical calculators (Ohm's law, cable sizing, voltage drop, fault current, motor FLC, PFC, and more)
Learning lessons on electricity fundamentals, three-phase, selectivity, harmonics, and more
Bill-of-materials, PDF, SVG, JSON export and QR-code sharing

solar_pv.title: Solar PV basics
solar_pv.description: Panels, MPPT, string vs micro-inverter — how a rooftop system turns sunlight into kilowatt-hours
solar_pv.intro: A solar PV system converts sunlight into DC, then an inverter turns it into grid-compatible AC. Output depends on panel wattage, count, daily sun hours, and system efficiency (dust, wiring loss, inverter). Three common topologies trade off cost, shade tolerance and monitoring granularity.

topologyExplain.string: One central inverter for all panels in a series string. Cheapest per watt, but shade on one panel drops the whole string.
topologyExplain.micro: One micro-inverter per panel. Handles per-panel shade well and gives per-panel monitoring, but ~30% more expensive.
topologyExplain.off_grid: PV + charge controller + battery bank + inverter. Independent from the grid — sizing must cover the worst-case day.

solar_pv.point1: Peak sun-hours (kWh/m²/day) vary by location — 3.5 in the UK, 4.5–5 in southern Europe, 6+ in Middle East and North Africa
solar_pv.point2: System efficiency is typically 75–85% after cable losses, MPPT losses, inverter losses, and soiling
solar_pv.point3: MPPT (Maximum Power Point Tracking) is what modern inverters do to squeeze the most watts out of variable panel V-I curves

ev_charging.title: EV charging (Mode / Type / kW)
ev_charging.description: Mode 1/2/3, Type 1/2 connectors, and the math behind charging times
ev_charging.intro: EV charging is standardised across three IEC "modes" that map to safety and communication: Mode 2 is the emergency cable, Mode 3 is a dedicated AC wallbox, DC fast is Mode 4 (CCS/CHAdeMO). Charge time = battery kWh / power kW, minus the 5–15 % that gets lost as heat.

modeExplain.mode2: Portable cable with an in-line control box — plugs into a normal socket. Slow (2–3 kW) but no installation. Meant as backup, not daily.
modeExplain.mode3: Dedicated wall-mounted AC unit — 7 kW (1-phase 32 A) up to 22 kW (3-phase 32 A). The standard home / workplace charger.
modeExplain.dc_fast: Public DC fast chargers (CCS, CHAdeMO) — 50 kW to 350 kW. Bypasses the on-board AC-DC converter for road-trip speeds.

ev_charging.point1: 3-phase charging = √3 × 400 × I ≈ 690 W per amp — much faster than single-phase for the same amp rating
ev_charging.point2: The car's on-board charger sets the AC ceiling — most 2020+ EVs are 11 kW; older ones cap at 3.6 or 7.4 kW
ev_charging.point3: Real-world DC fast charging slows dramatically above ~80 % state-of-charge to protect the battery — don't chase 100 %

ups_basics.title: UPS basics
ups_basics.description: Offline vs line-interactive vs online, kVA vs kW sizing, and runtime math
ups_basics.intro: An Uninterruptible Power Supply keeps critical loads alive during a mains outage. Three architectures trade off cost, transfer time, and how much conditioning the load actually sees. Runtime = (battery Ah × V × inverter efficiency) / load watts.

typeExplain.offline: Cheapest — mains passes through unless it fails, then flips to battery in ~5–10 ms. Fine for a home PC.
typeExplain.line_interactive: Adds AVR (auto voltage regulation) — cleans up sags/surges without switching to battery. Sweet spot for small servers.
typeExplain.online: Load is always powered from the inverter (battery in the middle). Zero transfer time and perfect sine wave — for medical / IT / industrial.

ups_basics.overload: ⚠ Load exceeds UPS real-power capacity (kVA × pf). Either downsize the load, raise the kVA rating, or move some circuits off this UPS.
ups_basics.point1: UPS ratings are in kVA (apparent power); real load capacity = kVA × PF, usually 0.7–0.9
ups_basics.point2: Runtime scales inversely with load — half the load = ~2× the runtime (not exactly, because Peukert's coefficient bites)
ups_basics.point3: Online UPS is the only architecture with truly zero transfer time — the others have 4–10 ms which is fine for computers but not for magnetics or motors

battery_chemistry.title: Battery chemistries compared
battery_chemistry.description: Li-ion, LiFePO4, lead-acid, Ni-MH — voltage, cycles, energy density, safety
battery_chemistry.intro: Not all batteries are equal. Chemistry sets the fundamental trade-offs: energy density (Wh/kg), cycle life, safety, cost, and self-discharge. Pick by application: a phone wants Li-ion, a home battery wants LiFePO4, a car starter wants lead-acid.

bestForText.lifepo4: Home solar batteries, e-bikes, marine — long life and safety trump weight
bestForText.liion: Phones, laptops, EVs, drones — anywhere weight matters most
bestForText.lead_acid: Car starter, UPS, forklift — cheap and rugged, high peak current
bestForText.nimh: AA / AAA rechargeables, hybrid cars — safe and forgiving

battery_chemistry.point1: LiFePO4 has 3–5× the cycle life of NMC Li-ion — worth the lower energy density for stationary storage
battery_chemistry.point2: Lead-acid is dead cheap but heavy and only ~50 % usable depth-of-discharge without killing cycles
battery_chemistry.point3: Ni-MH self-discharges fast (20 %/mo) — don't leave charged packs on the shelf for months

bonding_earthing.title: Bonding vs earthing
bonding_earthing.description: Both use green-yellow wire, both go to earth — but they solve different problems
bonding_earthing.intro: Earthing (grounding) is one wire from the appliance chassis to the earth electrode — it gives fault current a path to trip the RCD or MCB. Bonding is a wire between metal parts that are already there for other reasons — pipes, structural steel — to hold them all at the same potential so touching two of them can't shock you. Different job, different wire, both mandatory.

modeExplain.earthing: The appliance PE has a path to earth — good — but pipes and structure sit at a different potential. Touching the appliance and a pipe at the same time could still shock you.
modeExplain.bonding: The pipes are all at the same potential — good — but there's no fault path back to trip protection. A live-chassis fault would sit undetected.
modeExplain.both: The correct installation. Earthing gives the fault current somewhere to go (RCD trips); bonding equalises everything metallic so no dangerous voltage develops between touchable surfaces.

bonding_earthing.point1: Earthing = protective (creates a fault path). Bonding = equipotential (removes voltage between metal parts)
bonding_earthing.point2: In a bathroom the two are equally important — soaked skin plus a small potential difference is dangerous
bonding_earthing.point3: Green/yellow wire is used for both, but a bonding conductor is sized to the local metal work, not the supply cable

spd_lightning.title: Lightning & SPD (Type 1/2/3)
spd_lightning.description: Type 1 at the origin, Type 2 in the panel, Type 3 at sensitive loads — the surge cascade
spd_lightning.intro: A lightning strike doesn't have to hit your house to damage it — a nearby strike induces thousands of volts on nearby cables. Surge Protection Devices divert that transient to earth before it reaches sensitive electronics. IEC 61643 defines three types by mounting location and energy capacity.

explain.t1: For buildings with an external lightning protection system (rod on the roof). Handles the direct-strike energy on 10/350 µs impulse. Mounted at the service entry.
explain.t2: The everyday SPD — installed in the main consumer unit. Clips induced surges from nearby strikes. Must be paired with a T1 upstream if the building is exposed.
explain.t3: Fine-clamp SPD close to sensitive loads (server rack, medical, entertainment). Used in cascade after T2 to knock the voltage down further.

spd_lightning.point1: SPDs are consumables — they degrade with each surge. Look for a status window and replace when it turns red
spd_lightning.point2: SPD needs a good earth to work — poor earthing multiplies Up and reduces protection
spd_lightning.point3: Coordination matters: T1 must fire before T2, T2 before T3. Manufacturer tables spell out the coordination distance

afdd.title: Arc Fault Detection (AFDD)
afdd.description: Detects the RF signature of an electrical arc — the fire risk MCBs and RCDs miss
afdd.intro: Arc faults happen when a wire is loose, damaged, or a plug is worn — a tiny arc jumps the gap without drawing enough current to trip an MCB or the leakage to trip an RCD, but the arc temperature can start a fire. An AFDD watches the current waveform for the high-frequency signature of arcing and trips within milliseconds.

status.clean: ✓ Nominal — smooth sine, no arc detected
status.series_arc: ⚠ Series arc — random dropouts at zero-crossing. AFDD would trip.
status.parallel_arc: ⚠ Parallel arc — high-current spikes. AFDD would trip.
status.harmonics: ✓ Harmonic-rich but stable — AFDD ignores non-linear loads (LED drivers, VFDs)

explain.series_arc: A loose terminal or broken strand causes intermittent arcing along the current path. Little current change but big fire risk.
explain.parallel_arc: Damaged insulation causes arcing between conductors. High peak currents but often below the MCB's instantaneous trip.
explain.harmonics: Modern electronics draw non-sinusoidal current. An AFDD's algorithm has to distinguish 'noisy but safe' from 'arc-fault'.

afdd.point1: AFDD covers a fire hazard neither MCB (needs overload) nor RCD (needs earth leak) can see
afdd.point2: IEC 60364-4-42 and NEC 210.12 now require AFDDs in bedrooms and other high-risk circuits
afdd.point3: AFDD often combines AF + MCB + RCD in one 2-module device — pricier, but replaces three devices

reactive_power.title: Reactive power (kW / kVA / kVAR)
reactive_power.description: The power triangle, cos φ, and why the utility bills you for kVA on big loads
reactive_power.intro: Not all the power a load draws does work. The current flowing to a motor or transformer includes a chunk that goes back and forth building magnetic fields — reactive power (VAR). Real power (W) does the actual job. Apparent power (VA) is what the cables and generators have to carry. cos φ is the ratio of real to apparent — the closer to 1, the more efficient.
reactive_power.point1: P = S · cos φ, Q = S · sin φ, S² = P² + Q² — the power triangle
reactive_power.point2: Adding capacitors (PFC) supplies the reactive current locally so it doesn't flow all the way from the generator
reactive_power.point3: Bad PF doesn't cost energy directly — it costs cable capacity and generator capacity. Utilities bill big loads by kVA, not kW

insulation_types.title: Cable insulation types
insulation_types.description: PVC, XLPE, LSZH, rubber — temperature ratings, fire behaviour, when to use each
insulation_types.intro: The insulation around a conductor decides how hot it can run, how it behaves in a fire, and where you're allowed to install it. Four families dominate: PVC (cheap and everywhere), XLPE (higher temp), LSZH (public buildings), rubber (flexible and industrial).
insulation_types.fire.xlpe: Self-extinguishing, tougher than PVC at high temps
insulation_types.fire.lszh: Low smoke, zero halogen — safe for enclosed public spaces
insulation_types.fire.rubber: Depends on compound — most are self-extinguishing

explain.pvc: The default for indoor wiring. Cheap, easy to strip, good enough for 70 °C circuits. Don't use where smoke inhalation is a hazard.
explain.xlpe: Cross-linked polyethylene — handles 90 °C, better ampacity in the same cross-section. Standard for feeders and outdoor cables.
explain.lszh: Halogen-free jacket — no toxic smoke in a fire. Mandatory in tunnels, airports, hospitals, cruise ships.
explain.rubber: Very flexible and abrasion-resistant. Used on portable tools, welders, stage lighting — anywhere the cable moves.

insulation_types.point1: PVC is the default; XLPE when you need higher ampacity; LSZH when smoke is the hazard; rubber when flexibility is
insulation_types.point2: Max conductor temperature sets the ampacity table — XLPE at 90 °C carries ~15 % more current than PVC at 70 °C
insulation_types.point3: Never install PVC in a plenum or crawl space where a fire would trap the toxic smoke

ip_ratings.title: IP ratings — enclosures for the environment
ip_ratings.description: IP20 vs IP44 vs IP65/67 — what the two digits actually mean
ip_ratings.intro: IEC 60529 uses IP + 2 digits to describe an enclosure's resistance to solids (first digit, 0–6) and liquids (second digit, 0–9). Higher numbers = better protection. Pick the wrong rating for the location and you'll be rebuilding after the first rainy season.

liquidValues.immersion: 7 — immersion up to 1 m for 30 min

suitability.indoor_dry: Living rooms, offices, dry indoor spaces

ip_ratings.point1: IP20 is fine indoors; IP44 for bathrooms and covered outdoor; IP65 for exposed outdoor sockets
ip_ratings.point2: The 2nd digit tests are cumulative — an IP68 device also passes IP67, IP66, IP65, and so on
ip_ratings.point3: IP69K exists as an extension — high-temp, high-pressure jets for wash-down industries (food processing, mining)

star_delta.title: Motor star vs delta connection
star_delta.description: Same windings, two ways to connect them — different voltage, current, torque
star_delta.intro: A 3-phase induction motor has three windings. Connect their ends into a common point → star (Y). Connect them tail-to-head in a loop → delta (Δ). Same motor, but star sees phase voltage (√3× less) so each winding runs at 1/√3 the current — used for soft-starting or lower-power operation.

explain.star: Each winding sees phase voltage (230 V in a 400 V system). Lower current, lower torque — ideal for starting a motor before switching to Δ.
explain.delta: Each winding sees line voltage (400 V). Full torque and full current — normal running mode for motors marked '400 V Δ'.

star_delta.point1: Delta current = √3 × Star current for the same voltage — Y-Δ starting cuts inrush to ~1/3
star_delta.point2: Whether Y or Δ is 'normal' depends on the nameplate — a '230/400 V, Δ/Y' motor runs in Δ on 230 V systems, Y on 400 V
star_delta.point3: The star point can be brought out as a 4th terminal — that's the neutral for 3-phase 4-wire systems

rc_time_constant.title: RC charging (time constant τ)
rc_time_constant.description: Capacitor voltage vs time — the universal 63 % / 5τ rule
rc_time_constant.intro: When you close a switch to charge a capacitor through a resistor, the voltage doesn't jump to the supply — it climbs exponentially. The time constant τ = R × C tells you the pace: after 1τ the cap is 63 % charged, after 5τ it's 99 % done. The same maths governs discharging, RC filters, and every 555-timer circuit.
rc_time_constant.point1: τ (in seconds) = R (in Ω) × C (in F). 10 kΩ × 100 µF = 1 second
rc_time_constant.point2: After 1τ = 63 %; 2τ = 86 %; 3τ = 95 %; 5τ = 99 % — same shape regardless of scale
rc_time_constant.point3: RC filters use this same exponential — a low-pass filter's cutoff is 1 / (2π · RC)

fault_tree.title: "My breaker keeps tripping" — a diagnostic tree
fault_tree.description: Answer yes/no to symptoms and land on the likely cause + first-response action
fault_tree.intro: A tripped breaker is the safety system doing its job. But which job? Overload, short circuit, earth leakage, surge damage, or nuisance-tripping? Walk through the questions below — each answer narrows the fault space until one candidate is left.

questions.q_immediately: Does the breaker trip immediately when you reset it — even with everything unplugged?
questions.q_hot_wire: Do you see burn marks, smell melted plastic, or find a hot wire?
questions.q_after_appliance: Does it trip only after plugging in / turning on a specific appliance?
questions.q_rcd_only: Is it the RCD (not the MCB) that trips?
questions.q_after_storm: Did it first happen after a lightning storm or grid glitch?

r_short.title: Short circuit
r_short.desc: L touches N or PE somewhere on the fixed wiring. The MCB trips instantly on magnetic detection.
r_short.action: De-energise the circuit at the panel. Do NOT reset until you've traced and repaired the fault — usually a nail through a cable or a burnt junction box.

r_overload.title: Overload on that appliance
r_overload.desc: A specific appliance draws more than the circuit's rating (or the MCB's curve).
r_overload.action: Move the appliance to a higher-rated circuit, replace with a lower-power model, or upgrade the circuit cable + MCB together (never the MCB alone).

r_leakage.title: Earth leakage
r_leakage.desc: Current is escaping to earth — wet appliance, damaged insulation, or a nuisance-cumulative leak.
r_leakage.action: Unplug everything on the RCD, reset it, then plug loads in one by one until it trips again. That's your culprit.

r_surge_damage.title: Surge damaged the breaker
r_surge_damage.desc: A lightning-induced spike destroyed the breaker or a downstream device — sometimes it trips because it can no longer hold contact.
r_surge_damage.action: Replace the tripped breaker. Then install an SPD (Type 2 minimum) so the next surge is absorbed instead of destroying protection.

r_nuisance.title: Nuisance trip
r_nuisance.desc: Motor inrush, cold-filament bulbs, or a cumulative harmonic overload can trip C-curve breakers.
r_nuisance.action: Try a D-curve (or higher-rated same-cable) breaker for motor circuits. Or spread loads across more MCBs so no single one sees the whole inrush.

fault_tree.point1: Immediate re-trip = short circuit. Slow re-trip after minutes = overload. RCD-only = earth leakage. That's 90 % of the tree
fault_tree.point2: Always fix the ROOT CAUSE. Replacing an MCB with a bigger one just moves the fire risk to the cable
fault_tree.point3: If you can't isolate the fault safely, call a licensed electrician. Fault-finding on live circuits is not DIY territory

nameplate.title: Reading a nameplate
nameplate.description: Motor, MCB, transformer — decode the numbers stamped on the plate
nameplate.intro: Every electrical device carries a small metal or laminated plate with its critical ratings. Learn to read it and you can size cables, pick protection, and diagnose failures without a datasheet. Tap the fields below to see what each stamp means.
nameplate.tapHint: Tap a marker on the plate to see what that stamp means.

motor.power.label: Mechanical output power
motor.power.desc: The shaft power the motor delivers under nominal load, in kW or HP. Electrical input = P / (η · cos φ).

motor.rpm.label: Nominal speed
motor.rpm.desc: Rotor speed at rated load. Synchronous speed = 60·f/pole-pairs; nameplate is 2–5 % slower due to slip.

motor.voltage.label: Voltage & connection
motor.voltage.desc: Voltage the windings expect and how to connect them. '400 V Δ' = delta on a 400 V system; '230/400 V Δ/Y' = both wiring options.

motor.current.label: Full-load current (FLC)
motor.current.desc: Line current at rated load — used to size the cable, MCB and thermal overload.

motor.pf.label: Power factor
motor.pf.desc: Ratio of real to apparent power at full load. Lower PF = more reactive current for the same shaft power.

motor.freq.label: Rated frequency
motor.freq.desc: 50 or 60 Hz. A 60 Hz motor on 50 Hz runs slower and hotter (V/Hz mismatch).

motor.class.label: Insulation class & efficiency
motor.class.desc: F = insulation good up to 155 °C. IE3 = high-efficiency class (IEC 60034-30).

motor.ip.label: IP rating
motor.ip.desc: Enclosure protection — see the IP ratings lesson. IP55 = dust-protected + jet-water.

mcb.rating.label: Rated current In
mcb.rating.desc: Current the breaker carries indefinitely. Cable ampacity must exceed this at the installation conditions.

mcb.curve.label: Trip curve
mcb.curve.desc: B (3–5×In), C (5–10×In), D (10–20×In) — determines how quickly the magnetic trip fires vs inrush current.

mcb.icu.label: Breaking capacity Icu
mcb.icu.desc: Maximum short-circuit current the MCB can safely interrupt without welding shut. Must exceed your fault current.

mcb.voltage.label: Voltage rating
mcb.voltage.desc: Nominal 1-phase / 3-phase supply the MCB is designed for.

mcb.standard.label: Compliance standard
mcb.standard.desc: EN 60898 for household; EN 60947-2 for industrial. Determines test conditions.

transformer.kva.label: Apparent power rating
transformer.kva.desc: Design load in kVA. Real power = kVA × PF. Sets the maximum thermal capacity.

transformer.voltage.label: Voltage ratio
transformer.voltage.desc: Primary / secondary no-load voltage — e.g. 20 kV MV to 400 V LV.

transformer.current.label: Rated currents
transformer.current.desc: Full-load current on each winding. Used to size cables and protection.

transformer.uk.label: Short-circuit impedance
transformer.uk.desc: Percentage voltage drop at full load. Sets both the voltage regulation and the prospective fault current.

transformer.vector.label: Vector group
transformer.vector.desc: e.g. Dyn11 = delta primary, star secondary with neutral, 30° lag. Determines parallel-operation compatibility.

transformer.cooling.label: Cooling method
transformer.cooling.desc: ONAN = Oil Natural Air Natural. First letter oil, second air, third natural/forced.

nameplate.point1: The nameplate is a promise — the manufacturer says the device will work under exactly these conditions. Derate below them and it lasts longer
nameplate.point2: Voltage/frequency mismatch kills motors — 50 Hz motor on 60 Hz runs 20 % faster; 60 Hz on 50 Hz overheats
nameplate.point3: MCB Icu must exceed your prospective fault current — see the upstream_fault calculator

multimeter.title: Multimeter basics + CAT ratings
multimeter.description: Modes, safety categories, and common mistakes that cost meters (or fingers)
multimeter.intro: A multimeter measures voltage, current, resistance, continuity, and diode drop. Pick the wrong mode and you'll blow a fuse (best case) or the meter (worst). Pick the wrong CAT rating and the meter can literally explode. Learn the modes and the safety class before you probe a live circuit.

explain.vac: AC voltage — measures 230 V mains, 24 V AC control, etc. Highest scale first, then step down.
explain.vdc: DC voltage — batteries, DC bench supplies, PV panels. Watch polarity for older analog meters.
explain.a: Current — must be in SERIES with the circuit. Move the red probe to the 10 A jack. Common mistake: leaving probe in A jack and measuring V — shorts the source.
explain.ohm: Resistance — power the circuit OFF first. Meter injects a tiny current and measures the voltage drop.
explain.diode: Diode forward-drop — 0.6–0.7 V for silicon, 0.2–0.4 V for Schottky. Reverse shows 'OL' (open loop).
explain.continuity: Beeps if resistance < ~50 Ω. Fastest way to trace a broken wire or check a fuse.

multimeter.catExplain: CAT II = plug-in appliances, CAT III = distribution boards, CAT IV = service entrance. Use the wrong category near mains and the meter's fuse (or you) becomes the sacrificial part.
multimeter.point1: Red probe in the A jack + measuring voltage = short circuit. Always check the jack before you touch the probes
multimeter.point2: CAT rating scales with prospective fault energy — always use a CAT III/1000 V meter on distribution panels
multimeter.point3: Trust true-RMS meters on modern non-sinusoidal loads (LED, VFD, computers) — average-responding meters lie by 10–40 %

reading_diagrams.title: Reading a wiring diagram
reading_diagrams.description: Symbol conventions, line types, IEC vs ANSI — the alphabet of every diagram
reading_diagrams.intro: Wiring diagrams use a compact symbolic language so a whole installation fits on one page. Two families dominate: IEC (Europe/most of the world) and ANSI (North America). Same components, different squiggles. Learn to recognise both and every diagram becomes readable.
reading_diagrams.point1: IEC uses rectangles for resistors; ANSI uses zig-zags — same meaning, different symbol
reading_diagrams.point2: Solid lines are wires; dashed lines mean mechanical or logical (not electrical) coupling
reading_diagrams.point3: A dot at a wire crossing = connection; no dot = the wires cross without touching

wire_colors.title: Wire colors (L / N / PE by region)
wire_colors.description: The colour code changes between EU, US and legacy UK — know all three
wire_colors.intro: Wire colours identify the role of each conductor at a glance. The rules are regional: modern EU (harmonised HD 308), US (NEC), and pre-2004 UK differ significantly. Miswiring can be lethal — always verify before you touch.

notes.eu: EU harmonised — brown/black/grey lines, blue neutral, green-yellow PE. Same across Germany, France, most of Europe, Russia (GOST) and Armenia.
notes.us: US NEC: black + red + blue for 3-phase, white neutral, green/bare copper PE. High-leg delta uses orange for the wild leg.
notes.oldUk: Legacy UK (pre-2004): red/yellow/blue phases with black neutral. Still found in old buildings — always confirm with a tester.

wire_colors.point1: Green/yellow stripe is reserved for PE (protective earth) worldwide — never use it for anything else
wire_colors.point2: Blue = neutral in EU, but blue = a phase in the US — don't assume across borders
wire_colors.point3: Old installations often mix codes — a tester on every conductor before you touch it is not optional

contactor.title: How a contactor works
contactor.description: Coil energised = main contacts close, aux NC opens — the workhorse of motor control
contactor.intro: A contactor is a heavy-duty relay: a small coil current pulls a magnetic core that snaps the main power contacts closed. The main contacts (typically 3 poles for 3-phase) carry the load current; auxiliary contacts (NO or NC) signal the state of the coil so downstream control logic knows whether the contactor is on.
contactor.on: ✓ Coil energised — main contacts closed, load powered, aux NC opened
contactor.off: Coil de-energised — main contacts open, aux NC closed
contactor.point1: A tiny 24 V coil current can switch tens of amps at 400 V — that's the point of a contactor
contactor.point2: Auxiliary NC (95-96) is the standard interlock terminal for the coil circuit — used in start/stop stations
contactor.point3: Choose the coil voltage to match your control circuit (24 V DC, 230 V AC…) — the main contacts are voltage-agnostic

transformer_basics.title: Transformer basics
transformer_basics.description: Turns ratio, voltage/current inversion, and why power is (almost) conserved
transformer_basics.intro: A transformer trades voltage for current — or vice versa — through the ratio of primary to secondary turns. Double the turns on the secondary and you get double the voltage but half the current. Power stays constant (ideal transformer), which is why the grid uses high voltage: same power, thinner cables, less loss.
transformer_basics.powerBalance: Power balance (ideal): Pp = {{pp}} W ≈ Ps = {{ps}} W
transformer_basics.point1: Ideal ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is — voltage scales with turns, current scales inversely
transformer_basics.point2: Transformers work only with AC — DC would just heat the primary coil and go nowhere
transformer_basics.point3: Real transformers have ~95–99% efficiency; the losses are copper (I²R) + iron (eddy + hysteresis)

electricity_intro.title: What is electricity?
electricity_intro.description: Electrons flowing through a wire — the basics, illustrated
electricity_intro.intro: Electricity is the flow of electrons through a metal wire. When you switch on a lamp, the power source "pushes" electrons along the wire, and they transfer energy to the lamp so it lights up.
electricity_intro.watch: Watch the electrons speed up as you raise the voltage.
electricity_intro.point2: Current (A) measures how many electrons pass every second
electricity_intro.point3: Resistance slows the flow — like a narrowing in the wire

ohms_law.title: Ohm's Law · V = I × R
ohms_law.description: Interactive sliders showing how voltage, current and resistance are linked
ohms_law.intro: Ohm's law is the most important formula in electrical engineering. It links voltage (V), current (I) and resistance (R). Change any value and watch the others adjust.
ohms_law.point1: V = I × R — raise any two, the third follows
ohms_law.point2: Double R — current halves (at the same V)
ohms_law.point3: Double V — current doubles (at the same R)

series_parallel.title: Series vs Parallel
series_parallel.description: Compare the two topologies with a tap
series_parallel.intro: Resistors (or lamps) can be wired in two fundamental ways: in series (one after another) or in parallel (side by side). Each behaves very differently.
series_parallel.point3: Parallel: one dies, the rest keep working. Series: one dies, everything stops.

ac_vs_dc.title: AC vs DC — Alternating & Direct current
ac_vs_dc.description: See how sine waves change with frequency
ac_vs_dc.intro: Direct current (DC) flows one way only — from batteries or solar panels. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction 50 or 60 times per second (50 Hz in Europe/Armenia/Russia, 60 Hz in the US). AC is easier to step up and down with transformers, which is why the grid uses it.
ac_vs_dc.point1: DC — batteries, electronics (5 V, 12 V, 24 V)
ac_vs_dc.point2: AC — mains 230 V / 50 Hz, industrial 400 V
ac_vs_dc.point3: Transformers only work with AC — that's why the grid uses AC

components.title: Electronic components
components.description: Meet the building blocks: resistors, capacitors, diodes, LEDs, transistors, ICs
components.intro: Every circuit is built from a handful of primitive components. Tap each one below to see how it looks and what it does.

resistor.name: Resistor
resistor.description: A component that opposes current flow, dissipating energy as heat. Value in Ω (ohms).
resistor.usedFor: limiting current to LEDs, voltage dividers, pull-up/pull-down

capacitor.name: Capacitor
capacitor.description: Stores electric charge between two plates. Value in F (farads), typically µF or nF.
capacitor.usedFor: smoothing power supplies, filtering signals, timing circuits

inductor.name: Inductor
inductor.description: A coil that stores energy in a magnetic field. Value in H (henries), typically mH or µH.
inductor.usedFor: filtering, switching power supplies, RF circuits, transformers

diode.name: Diode
diode.description: Lets current flow only in one direction. The arrow shows the allowed direction.

led.name: LED
led.description: A diode that emits light when current flows through it. Needs a series resistor.

transistor.name: Transistor
transistor.description: A tiny switch or amplifier — a small current at the Base controls a much larger one from Collector to Emitter.

ic.name: Integrated circuit (IC)
ic.description: Millions of components packed onto one silicon chip. The 555 is a classic timer IC.

battery.name: Battery
battery.description: Chemically stores energy and releases it as DC current. Rated in V and mAh/Ah.
battery.usedFor: portable power for anything from a torch to a phone to an EV

components.point1: Passive components (R, C, L) don't need power to work — they just react
components.point2: Active components (diodes, transistors, ICs) need power and can amplify or switch signals
components.point3: Every gadget is just clever combinations of these blocks

fuses.title: Fuses & MCBs
fuses.description: Watch a fuse blow / MCB trip when the current gets too high
fuses.intro: A fuse or MCB is a sacrificial safety device — it interrupts the circuit before the wires overheat and start a fire. Choose a rating that matches the cable, then push the current above the trip point.
fuses.overloading: Overloading! Load exceeds {{rating}}A — the device will trip soon.
fuses.tripped: MCB tripped ({{rating}}A) — reset the toggle to restore power.
fuses.blown: Fuse blown ({{rating}}A) — replace the fuse element.
fuses.point1: The fuse rating must match the cable ampacity, not the load — otherwise the cable burns before the fuse blows
fuses.point2: MCBs are reusable (just flip the toggle back up); fuses must be replaced
fuses.point3: Curve C MCBs handle short inrush currents (motors, transformers) without nuisance-tripping

rcd_earth.title: RCD & earthing (life-safety)
rcd_earth.description: Slide the leakage current up — the RCD trips before you get shocked
rcd_earth.intro: An RCD detects the tiny current that escapes to earth when someone touches a live wire, and cuts power in ~40 ms. The earth wire on your appliances gives that current an easy path away from the person. Together they're a life-saving pair.
rcd_earth.danger: ⚡ Shock! Without an earth wire the current flows through the person — the RCD hasn't tripped yet.
rcd_earth.rcdSaved: RCD tripped — power off. The RCD just saved someone's life.
rcd_earth.safeState: Everything nominal — leakage below trip threshold.
rcd_earth.point1: RCDs trip on residual (out-of-balance) current, not overcurrent — a totally different job from an MCB
rcd_earth.point2: Bathrooms and outdoor sockets use 10 mA RCDs for extra safety around water
rcd_earth.point3: The earth wire is not decorative — it's the reason the RCD trips fast enough to save you

batteries.title: Batteries: series vs parallel
batteries.description: Series adds voltage, parallel adds capacity
batteries.intro: Chain batteries end-to-end and their voltages add. Wire them side-by-side and their capacity (mAh) adds instead. Which one you need depends on whether the load wants more push (V) or more staying power (mAh).
batteries.point1: Series: V adds, mAh stays the same → higher voltage, same battery life
batteries.point2: Parallel: mAh adds, V stays the same → longer life, same voltage
batteries.point3: Never mix old + new cells or different brands — the weakest one becomes a load and can leak

grounding.title: Earthing systems — TN, TT, IT
grounding.description: The 5 IEC earthing arrangements — what changes and why it matters
grounding.intro: The IEC defines five ways to reference an installation to earth: TN-C, TN-S, TN-C-S, TT, and IT. The choice affects which protective device works, how fast a fault clears, and whether extra bonding is needed. Tap each one to see how the neutral, protective earth (PE) and appliance chassis are wired.

tn_c.name: TN-C — combined PEN
tn_c.description: Neutral and protective earth share one conductor (PEN) all the way from the transformer to the appliance.
tn_c.pros: Cheap — one wire less to run.
tn_c.cons: PEN break = live chassis; RCDs cannot detect leakage. Banned in new residential installs.

tn_s.name: TN-S — separate N and PE
tn_s.description: Neutral and PE are separate all the way from the source. Classic modern layout.
tn_s.pros: Clean and safe — RCDs work, no PEN-break risk.
tn_s.cons: Needs a proper PE conductor back to the source (extra copper).

tn_cs.name: TN-C-S — split near the load
tn_cs.description: PEN comes from the transformer, splits into N and PE at the consumer unit. Common in UK / Europe.
tn_cs.pros: Compromise: less copper upstream, safe PE downstream.
tn_cs.cons: PEN break upstream still dangerous. Requires solid main earth bond.

tt.name: TT — independent local earth
tt.description: Utility neutral not distributed as PE; each installation has its own earth electrode.
tt.pros: Isolated from utility PEN faults. Rural / small-village standard.
tt.cons: High loop impedance — RCDs are mandatory; MCBs alone won't disconnect for earth faults.

it.name: IT — isolated (or impedance)
it.description: Utility neutral isolated (or connected to earth via high impedance). Fault currents on first fault are very small.
it.pros: First earth fault does not trip → continuity of service (hospitals, ships, mines).
it.cons: Requires insulation-monitoring device (IMD); complex; installers must be trained.

grounding.point1: The earthing system dictates which fault-protection strategy the installation needs — MCB alone, RCD, or both
grounding.point2: TT is common in rural areas because the utility doesn't run PE — you need a local earth rod
grounding.point3: IT keeps the lights on after a first fault — critical for hospitals & industrial process plants

selectivity.title: MCB selectivity (coordination)
selectivity.description: Upstream vs downstream trip curves — will only the faulted circuit disconnect?
selectivity.intro: Selectivity (a.k.a. discrimination) means only the breaker closest to the fault opens — the upstream one stays on. In a family home you don't want a short in one lamp to darken the whole apartment. Plot the two trip curves on a log-log chart and see whether the downstream curve is entirely under the upstream one.
selectivity.selective: ✓ Selective — only the {{downstream}} A breaker will trip at this fault current
selectivity.not_selective: ⚠ Not selective — both breakers will trip. Upstream {{upstream}} A is too small compared to downstream {{downstream}} A.
selectivity.neither: Fault too small — neither breaker will trip yet
selectivity.partial: Partial selectivity — behaviour depends on exact conditions
selectivity.point1: General rule: upstream rating ≥ 1.6 × downstream. E.g. 40 A upstream, 25 A downstream ✓
selectivity.point2: Selectivity fails at very high fault currents — both magnetic trips fire together
selectivity.point3: For guaranteed selectivity use Siemens/ABB "selective" (S-type) MCBs or a matched cascade table

motor_start.title: Motor starting methods
motor_start.description: DOL, Star-Delta, Soft-starter, VFD — inrush current side by side
motor_start.intro: A three-phase motor draws 5–8× its full-load current during start-up (locked-rotor current, LRA). That short-lived spike can dip the voltage across the whole panel or trip protection devices. Different start methods trade start-up torque for gentler inrush.
motor_start.point1: DOL: cheapest, brutal inrush — fine for small motors < 4 kW
motor_start.point2: Star-Delta: ~1/3 inrush, less torque, needs 6-wire motor & contactor set
motor_start.point3: VFD: smoothest start & full torque control, but expensive and adds harmonic distortion

harmonics.title: Harmonic distortion (THD)
harmonics.description: Non-linear loads pollute the sine wave — see the distortion & THD %
harmonics.intro: LED drivers, VFDs, computer power supplies and other switch-mode loads draw current in short pulses instead of a smooth sine. Fourier's theorem tells us that pulse is really a sum of the fundamental (50/60 Hz) plus higher-frequency "harmonics" — the 3rd, 5th, 7th and so on. Add enough of them and the neutral wire carries the sum of the 3rd harmonics from all three phases (they don't cancel like the fundamental).
harmonics.good: ✓ Waveform stays clean — THD within IEEE 519 limits
harmonics.bad: ⚠ Heavy distortion — neutral overheating, meter errors, protection nuisance-trips
harmonics.explain: Grid THD > 5 % (IEEE 519) or > 8 % (IEC 61000-2-4) causes reactive-power meter errors, capacitor bank overheating and transformer derating.
harmonics.point1: Triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, 15th) add up in the neutral instead of cancelling — double-size the neutral in datacentre feeders
harmonics.point2: Common culprits: LED lighting, VFDs, UPS, computers — anything with a diode-bridge front end
harmonics.point3: Fix with harmonic filters, K-rated transformers, or active PFC front ends on new equipment

vdrop_cascade.title: Cascading voltage drop
vdrop_cascade.description: Feeder → sub-panel → final circuit — the drops add up
vdrop_cascade.intro: Voltage drop isn't just one number — it's the sum across every conductor between the source and the load. If a feeder drops 2 %, a sub-panel drop 1.5 %, and a final circuit 2.5 %, the last socket sees 6 % less voltage. IEC 60364 caps that at 3 % for lighting and 5 % for other circuits.
vdrop_cascade.exceeds3: 3–5 % — OK for sockets, exceeds the 3 % lighting limit
vdrop_cascade.exceeds5: > 5 % — exceeds every IEC / BS 7671 limit — bump a cross-section up
vdrop_cascade.point1: Voltage drop scales linearly with current AND with length — halving one halves the drop
vdrop_cascade.point2: Cross-section (mm²) inversely affects drop — 2.5 mm² has twice the drop of 5 mm² for the same run
vdrop_cascade.point3: IEC / BS 7671 limits: 3 % for lighting, 5 % for other; measure at the far end, not just the panel

three_phase.title: Three-phase power
three_phase.description: Three sine waves 120° apart — the backbone of the electrical grid
three_phase.intro: The utility grid delivers three separate sine waves, each phase offset by 120°. If the three phases are perfectly balanced, the current in the neutral wire is zero. That's why factories and large buildings use three-phase — same power delivered with thinner cables.
three_phase.unbalanced: Unbalanced — neutral is carrying about {{current}} A
three_phase.point1: Line voltage (between phases) = √3 × phase voltage. In Europe: 400 V line, 230 V phase.
three_phase.point2: Balanced 3-phase loads (motors, heaters) don't need a neutral wire at all
three_phase.point3: Big residential meters count 3-phase energy — the more balanced your usage, the more efficient

breadboard.title: Build your own circuit
breadboard.description: Drag components onto a virtual breadboard — no wiring soldering, just play
breadboard.intro: A breadboard is a plastic grid full of tiny holes wired together in a fixed pattern. It lets you build a working circuit in minutes without soldering. Below is a simplified version — tap a component, then tap a hole to place it. Drag placed components to move them, or use the arrow keys after selecting.
breadboard.hint: Red rail = +, blue rail = −. Drag a placed component to move it. Tap once to select, then rotate/delete/nudge.

status.empty: Empty board — pick a component from above and tap a hole to place it.
status.need_battery: Add a battery — every circuit needs a power source.
status.need_led: Add an LED — the light needs somewhere to shine.
status.need_resistor: Add a resistor — LEDs need current-limiting or they burn out.
status.need_wires: Add wires — connect the components to the + and − rails to close the loop.
status.works: ✓ Nice! Your circuit has all the parts of a working LED lamp.
status.danger_multiple_batteries: Two batteries fighting — pick one power source and remove the other.

breadboard.point1: Breadboards have hidden internal wires — components in the same column connect automatically
breadboard.point2: Long horizontal rows on top / bottom are power (+) and ground (−) — like the app's mini rails
breadboard.point3: This is how every hobbyist tests a circuit before making a PCB
